question: What has to be true of the final forecast year before you can apply a terminal value to it?
model_answer_md:
It has to describe a business in **equilibrium**, because the perpetuity formula assumes that year repeats forever with only modest growth on top. Four things in particular.

**Capex ≈ D&A.** A company growing at the economy's rate is replacing what wears out, not expanding. If the final year still shows capex well above depreciation, you are capitalising a company that keeps investing heavily without the growth that investment should buy.

**Working capital growing only with revenue.** No step-changes in payment terms or inventory efficiency — those are one-offs and cannot repeat forever.

**Margins at a sustainable, mid-cycle level.** Not a peak. If the final year is a good year, the perpetuity assumes every year is a good year.

**Growth already faded** to the terminal rate, so there is no discontinuity between the last forecast year and the perpetuity.

Because the terminal value is usually three-quarters of the answer, an error here dominates everything else in the model.
key_points: The final year must represent a steady state, not a snapshot
Capex should have converged on D&A
Working capital grows in line with revenue, with no one-off improvements
Growth already faded to the terminal rate — no discontinuity

follow_ups.question: How would you handle a cyclical company?
follow_ups.answer_md: Normalise to mid-cycle explicitly. Take the average margin across a full cycle — often seven to ten years, covering at least one downturn — rather than whatever the final forecast year happens to show, and say clearly that this is what you have done. If the forecast ends near a peak, capitalising it assumes the peak is permanent and can overstate the value by a wide margin. Some practitioners extend the forecast so it ends at a genuine mid-cycle point, which is cleaner but requires forecasting the cycle itself.

follow_ups.question: What if the company will still be growing quickly in year five?
follow_ups.answer_md: Then year five is the wrong place to stop. Extend the explicit forecast until growth has faded — ten years is common for high-growth businesses — so the fade happens where it is visible and defensible rather than being handled by an abrupt jump into a 2 % perpetuity. Applying a terminal value to a company still compounding at 15 % implies an instantaneous collapse in growth that no business actually experiences, and it makes the terminal number essentially arbitrary.

weak_answer_note: Only mentioning growth and missing capex, working capital and margins. At this level the interviewer wants the full normalisation checklist, and specifically the capex-versus-D&A convergence, which is the one candidates most often omit.
